newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- EC'S VOTE BAN DELAYS LONRHO DEMERGER PLAN

The European Commission has imposed a ban on the main shareholder in Lonrho's mining and trading business, Anglo American, from voting its 28 percent stake in the company, thus delaying the demerger plan. The EC is investigating the companies' combined position in the world platinum market. Lonrho has said it is unwilling to hold a shareholder meeting, to vote on a split, at which its largest investor is barred from voting.
-- CREST TRAINS TEAMS OF TROUBLESHOOTERS

The electronic share settlement system, Crest, is using staff from the Stock Exchange, including stockbrokers and registrars, to help eliminate its performance problems. They will look for the causes of 30,000 share deals being held up and try to find defects in the users' computer systems. Chief executive Iain Saville claims that the performance of Crest is improving but warns that pressure will be increased by the greater number of shares on Crest and "bed-and-breakfast" deals to crystalise capital gains tax, by large share issues from building societies.
-- BROKER PREPARES TO PULL OUT OF LLOYD'S

An insurance brokerage chaired by Peter Nutting, who has been elected to the ruling council of Lloyd's of London, FMW International, is leaving the insurance organisation, saying it is too expensive. Mr Nutting said that FMW could save 200,000 stg a year in professional indemnity insurance coverage by opting for the more reasonable level demanded by the brokers' registration council. Leaving will also mean the broker will not have to contribute to the Lloyd's financial reorganisation.
THE TIMES
-- TUC FEARS WORKING TIME OPT-OUT WILL HIT HOLIDAYS

The TUC are to warn six million British workers they could lose holidays if the Government succeeds in opting-out from Europe's 48-hour week working time directive. The unions will say that the Government's move is "bad politics", and will affect 9,000 people in every constituency. Prime Minister John Major insists that Britain will not agree to any deal at the European Union's intergovernmental conference unless the UK's opt-out is extended.
-- JOB HOPES AT THEIR BEST FOR SEVEN YEARS

Manpower, the job agency, in its latest employment forecasts, say that Britain's job prospects now stand at a seven-year high, suggesting a "prosperous" start to the new year. The forecast comes in the wake of overall claimant unemployment falling, before the Christmas and New Year holiday, to below two million for the first time for six years. The Manpower survey suggests 21 percent of employers are forecasting an increase in job levels, with 15 percent foreseeing a fall.
-- IOD SAYS SINGLE CURRENCY THREATENS BRITAIN

The Institute of Directors has cautioned that joining the European single currency in 1997 would result in a threat to Britain's competitiveness. Director-general, Tim Melville-Ross, said important decisions concerning Britain's future in Europe would be made in the coming year. He also said that UK employment could be endangered by labour regulations set out in the social chapter of the Maastricht treaty.
THE GUARDIAN
-- G7 TO FOCUS ON CRISIS STATES

The G7 meeting next month between finance ministers of the group of seven richest industrial countries is set to concentrate on the growing risk of financial collapse in Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey. The G7 is determined to launch a pre-emptive strike against the mounting economic difficulties of problem countries rather than allowing another Mexican-style financial crisis, which could affect global financial stability.
-- STEEL FIRM HITS OUT IN TAKEOVER ROW

The steel castings company fighting a 58 million stg bid from engineering group Triplex Lloyd, William Cook, has complained to the Takeover Panel after Triplex questioned the accuracy of profit forecasts that Cook made before Christmas. Triplex accused William Cook over the feasibility with which the company had been able to come up with improved figures. William Cook urged shareholders not to be distracted by the claims.
-- REFORM GROUP LAYS OUT PLANS FOR STAKEHOLDER COMPANY RESULTS

If the Centre for Tomorrow's Company can force through its ideas on reporting to all stakeholders, company results could race a dramatic shake-up. The centre has set up a task force to redevelop the conventional annual report to consider the broader values backed by the Tomorrow's Company inquiry by the Royal Society for Arts two years ago. An alternative format will be based on measurements of social and financial performance, but will be less complex and costly than the audits produced by firms such as Body Shop.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- OFT TURNS UP HEAT OVER CODE OF PRACTICE

The Office of Fair Trading is putting pressure on gas and electricity regulators to come up with a tough enforceable code of practice aimed at stamping out dubious sales tactics by rival suppliers in the move towards full domestic competition planned for 1998. The OFT will bring together Ofgas and Offer at a private conference in January to discuss how a binding joint code could be developed.
-- FIRMS FACE SANCTIONS OVER PENSIONS

Johnstone Douglas, a pay and benefits firm that advises companies on how to convert their pension funds from final-salary to money-purchase schemes, has warned that thousands of small and medium-sized firms could face fines and other legal sanctions through failing to implement provisions of the new Pensions Act in April 1997. Among the most likely problems will be the failure to give members the option to nominate trustees, to appoint auditors to pension schemes, maintain up-to-date accounts and keep separate bank accounts for trustees.
-- 20 BILLION STG BONANZA FORECAST FOR NORTH SEA OIL

According to forecasts by the Inland Revenue, North Sea oil and gas revenues will contribute more than 20 billion stg to the Exchequer over the next six years. The Revenue's forecast is based on output remaining at similar levels to today, while oil and gas prices stay as at present. The figures come as a report by Royal Bank of Scotland shows that UK gas and oil production rose to its highest level since October 1995.
